newsitem.title: USA: U.S. House Democratic leader wants China MFN revoked.
newsitem.headline: U.S. House Democratic leader wants China MFN revoked.

text.p: U.S. House of Representatives Democratic Leader Richard Gephardt on Tuesday said President Bill Clinton has been "far too weak" on China's human rights record and urged Congress to revoke Chinese trading privileges.

"Our trade policy with China has failed," Gephardt said in a speech to the Economic Club of Detroit. "It has failed not only on moral grounds, but economically as well. There is nothing 'free' about our trade with China -- in fact it comes to us at great cost and little benefit."

Gephardt, a Missouri Democrat, denounced human rights violations by China's "totalitarian" leaders and said they should be linked to a new U.S. policy of "firm engagement" with China that demands improvements in human and worker rights.
He also said the U.S. trade deficit with China hit nearly $40 billion in 1996 and that it was likely to exceed $50 billion this year.

Revocation of China's most favored nation (MFN) trading status with the United States would cause duties on imports from China to soar to the high levels of the 1930s. Only a handful of countries do not enjoy MFN status.

Clinton announced on May 19 that he would renew MFN for China this year, and opponents were expected to mount the fiercest congressional fight over the issue in years. The House in 1996 voted 286-141 to renew the privileges.
News of Gephardt's position drew a swift response from White House spokesman Mike McCurry, who said "we'll charitably disagree" with the 11-term congressman from St. Louis.

Speaking in Paris, where Clinton signed a pact between NATO and Russia on European security, McCurry said, "The suspension of normal trade relations with China would be, in some sense, a declaration of economic war with China and would further isolate China from the world community."
Two Democratic lawmakers, Sen. Joseph Lieberman of Connecticut, and Rep. Bob Matsui of California, said they would support Clinton's renewal of MFN for China.

"The U.S.-China relationship is probably the most important bilateral relationship the United States will have over the next 25 years," said Matsui, the senior Democrat on the Ways and Means Trade subcommittee. "It is my opinion that if we cut off MFN with China it would be the equivalent of cutting off diplomatic relations."
But Gephardt stopped short of advocating a boycott of Chinese goods and said he would continue to encourage U.S. corporations to do business in China.

"I think that means we can continue to trade but on a different basis," he said at a news conference prior to the speech. "In other words, they would not experience the same tariff basis as other nations."

Gephardt, viewed as a leading contender to challenge Vice President Al Gore for his party's 2000 presidential nomination, also said China's trade policies, which include "blackmailing" companies into giving China technology and trade secrets, will turn it into an economic powerhouse.
Gephardt said that he has made no decision to run for president and "won't for a long time."

Continued oppression in China will keep Chinese wages at poverty levels, which in turn will put downward pressure on U.S. wages, Gephardt said. He said China should not be allowed to regain MFN status until it ends the sale of goods made by millions of people in forced labor camps and prisons.

Vice President Gore, visiting New Hampshire on Tuesday barely a week after Gephardt's second visit to the state, used humor to brush off questions about whether he and Gephardt would be opposing candidates for the Democratic nomination in 2000.
"Political questions like that are, in my view premature," Gore told reporters at one stop. Then he chuckled and added: "Because it's 987 days until the New Hampshire (primary), but who's counting?"
But asked about Gephardt's disagreements with the administration, Gore said:

"I don't think the American people think it is good for our country to have a continuous presidential campaign. There are issues discussed year in and year out ... I choose to defend the president's policies, not only because I agree with them and helped to shape them, but because I think the Clinton-Gore administration and its approach has been good for this country."
